title: HF, VHF and UHF in steps of ten
summary: The three range names are back to back, and each one ends where the next begins, ten times higher.
hook: Count by tens: 3, 30, 300, 3000 MHz. H, then V (very), then U (ultra).

title: Radio wave speed and wavelength
summary: Every radio wave moves at the same speed, so frequency alone sets the wavelength.

points.label: Which frequency is fastest
points.value: All travel at the same velocity

points.label: Formula
points.value: Wavelength in meters = 300 / frequency in MHz

hook: 300 shows up twice: waves move 300,000,000 meters per second, and wavelength in meters is 300 divided by MHz.

title: Polarization follows the electric field
summary: A radio wave has two fields at right angles. The electric field's direction is its polarization, and matching it matters.

points.label: Two parts of a radio wave
What sets polarization
points.value: The orientation of the electric field

points.label: VHF, UHF long-distance
points.value: Horizontal, for CW and SSB contacts

points.label: After the ionosphere
points.value: Elliptical, so vertical or horizontal both work

hook: Match polarization on direct VHF and UHF paths. Signals from the ionosphere are elliptical, so either one works.

title: Technician on HF versus above 30 MHz
summary: On HF a Technician gets a small slice of 10 meters at lower power. Above 30 MHz the power ceiling is much higher.
hook: On 10 meters, beacons sit at 28.200 to 28.300 MHz, right below the Technician phone slice at 28.300 to 28.500 MHz.

title: Landmarks on 6 and 2 meters
summary: A few frequencies tell you which band you are on, where CW only lives, and where to call on FM simplex.

points.label: CW only segments
points.value: 50.0 MHz to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 MHz to 144.1 MHz

points.label: SSB phone above 50 MHz
points.value: In at least some segment of every band

hook: 146.52 MHz is both the 2 meter answer and the national FM simplex calling frequency. The CW only slices start at 50.0 and 144.0 MHz.

title: License life cycle
summary: From the exam to renewal, the license follows a fixed timeline, and you only transmit while it is in the database and current.

points.label: Notice of your new license
points.value: Email from the FCC with a link to the grant

points.label: Proof of the grant
points.value: The license appears in the FCC ULS database

points.label: First transmission
points.value: As soon as the grant appears in the database

points.label: Transmit during grace?
points.value: No, wait until it is renewed

hook: Ten years on, renew up to 90 days early, two years of grace, but no transmitting while expired.

title: Control operator rules
summary: Every transmitting station needs a control operator. The licensee picks them, and their license class sets the privileges.

points.label: Control operator
points.value: Named by the licensee, responsible for the rules

points.label: Control point
points.value: Where the control operator function is performed

points.label: Tech in an Extra segment
points.value: At no time, other than an emergency

points.label: Who is responsible
points.value: The control operator and the station licensee

points.label: Via a satellite
points.value: Anyone allowed on the satellite uplink frequency

hook: The control operator's license, not the station owner's, decides what frequencies you may use.

title: Station types and kinds of control
summary: Part 97 names stations by what they do, and control can be remote or automatic.

points.label: Repeater station
points.value: Retransmits another station on another channel

points.label: Auxiliary station
points.value: One-way link, remote receiver to main repeater

points.label: Space station
points.value: More than 50 km above Earth's surface

points.label: Remote control example
points.value: Operating the station over the internet

points.label: Repeater relays a violation
points.value: Control operator of the originating station

hook: Repeaters run on automatic control. If one relays a violation, the control operator of the station that sent it is accountable.

title: Station identification rules
summary: One timing rule covers almost everything: your call sign every 10 minutes and at the end. Only model craft control is exempt.

points.label: How often
points.value: At least every 10 minutes and at the end

points.label: Method on phone
points.value: Call sign by CW or phone emission

hook: Every 10 minutes and at the end, even when using tactical calls like Race Headquarters. Model craft control is the only time you skip it.

title: Forbidden content and narrow exceptions
summary: The default answer is no. Where a yes exists, it is tied to one narrow situation.

points.label: Broadcasting
points.value: Prohibited: aimed at the general public

points.label: Encoded messages
points.value: Only commands to space stations or model craft

points.label: Advertising gear for sale
points.value: Amateur gear, not on a regular basis

points.label: Getting paid
points.value: Part of classroom instruction at a school

points.label: Helping news gathering
points.value: Only for immediate safety of life or property

hook: Each yes is narrow: models and spacecraft, a classroom, the occasional gear sale, or safety of life.

title: International and third-party contacts
summary: Contacts abroad are fine within limits, and passing a message for someone else needs an agreement.

points.label: What you may talk about
points.value: Incidental to amateur purposes, personal remarks

points.label: Countries you can't contact
points.value: Any that notified the ITU it objects

points.label: Third-party communication
points.value: Message to another station for another person

points.label: Unlicensed guest abroad
points.value: Country must have a third-party agreement

hook: A third party is the person who isn't licensed. Abroad, their country needs a third-party agreement with the U.S.

title: RACES, ARES and emergency rules
summary: RACES is the civil defense service and needs certification. ARES is volunteers. FCC rules still apply in a crisis.

points.label: ARES
points.value: Volunteers who registered for public service

points.label: RACES
points.value: Part 97 civil defense service for emergencies

points.label: Outside your privileges?
points.value: Only for immediate safety of life or property

hook: RACES has the C for civil defense, so it is the one that needs certification.

title: How a net and its messages work
summary: A net control station runs the show, and formal messages (traffic) carry a header used to track them.

points.label: Net control station
points.value: Calls the net to order, directs check-ins

points.label: Your part in a net
points.value: Transmit only when directed, unless emergency

points.label: Traffic
points.value: Formal messages exchanged by net stations

points.label: Preamble
points.value: Information needed to track the message

points.label: Check
points.value: Number of words in the text

points.label: Unusual words
points.value: Spell them with a standard phonetic alphabet

title: Call sign order when calling
summary: When you reach for one station, say their call first and yours second.

points.label: Answering a CQ
points.value: Their call sign, then your call sign

points.label: Calling a known station
points.value: Their call sign, then your call sign

points.label: Open for a repeater contact
points.value: Your call sign, then the word listening

points.label: CQ without a repeater
points.value: CQ a few times, this is, your call, listen

hook: Them, then me. With no one in particular in mind, you give only your own call sign.

title: CQ and Q signals
summary: A few short codes save time on the air.

title: Repeater offsets and simplex
summary: A repeater listens on one frequency and talks on another. Simplex skips the repeater and uses one frequency.

points.label: Repeater offset
points.value: Gap between transmit and receive frequencies

points.label: Reverse function
points.value: Listen on the repeater's input frequency

points.label: Simplex
points.value: Transmit and receive on the same frequency

points.label: Why simplex channels exist
points.value: Talk directly without tying up a repeater

hook: Higher band, bigger offset: 600 kHz on 2 meters, 5 MHz on 70 centimeters.

title: Repeater tones and digital codes
summary: Analog repeaters open with tones. Digital radios need codes and IDs programmed in before you can use a repeater or group.

points.label: CTCSS
points.value: Sub-audible tone sent with your voice

points.label: DMR color code
points.value: Access code for a specific repeater

points.label: Joining a talkgroup
points.value: Program or enter the group's ID code

points.label: DMR code plug
points.value: Configuration data for repeaters and talkgroups

hook: Analog uses tones: one hidden tone (CTCSS) or two at once (DTMF). Digital uses codes you program in.

title: Multipath: many paths, one signal
summary: When copies of a signal arrive by different paths they add or cancel, which can hurt, but a reflection can also help.

points.label: Picket fencing
points.value: Rapid flutter on mobile signals from multipath

points.label: Effect on data
points.value: Error rates are likely to increase

points.label: Blocked path to a repeater
points.value: Find a path that reflects signals to it

title: Rain and leaves by frequency
summary: The higher the frequency, the more weather and vegetation get in the way.
hook: Little effect on 10 and 6 meters, real losses up at UHF and microwave.

title: The ionosphere: HF yes, UHF rarely
summary: The ionosphere carries HF signals long distances. It rarely helps UHF, and opens 6 and 10 meters near the sunspot peak.

points.label: UHF simplex range
points.value: Usually not propagated by the ionosphere

points.label: Best 10 meter F region time
points.value: Dawn to shortly after sunset, high sunspots

points.label: Irregular fading
points.value: Signals from different paths combine randomly

hook: At the sunspot peak, even 10 and 6 meters can go long distance via the F region.

title: VHF and UHF beyond the horizon
summary: VHF and UHF mostly travel line of sight, but several effects carry them farther. Match each effect to its clue.

points.label: Past the visual horizon
points.value: The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly

hook: Regular is tropo (temperature inversions). Occasional is Sporadic E. Raspy is aurora.

title: Electrical quantities and units
summary: Each quantity has its own unit and a one-line meaning. Learn them as pairs.

points.label: Voltage
points.value: A difference in it causes electron flow

points.label: Power
points.value: Watts: the rate electrical energy is used

points.label: Capacitance
points.value: Farad: stores energy in an electric field

points.label: Inductance
points.value: Henry: stores energy in a magnetic field

points.label: Impedance
points.value: Ohm: the opposition to AC current flow

hook: Capacitance goes with the electric field, inductance with the magnetic field.

title: Small prefixes: milli, micro, pico
summary: Milli means thousandths and micro means millionths. Shift the decimal three places per step.

points.label: Micro means
points.value: Millionths: one one-millionth of a volt

hook: A thousand milli make one whole; a million micro make one whole.

title: Big prefixes: kilo, mega, giga
summary: Each step up (kilo, mega, giga) is a thousand times bigger, so the decimal moves three places.

points.label: Kilo means
points.value: One thousand: one kilovolt is one thousand volts

hook: Up a prefix, decimal three places left: 2425 MHz is 2.425 GHz. Down a prefix, three places right: 3.525 MHz is 3525 kHz.

title: Decibel ladder
summary: A few power ratios cover the decibel questions: double, quarter, and ten times.
hook: Each doubling adds 3 dB and each halving takes 3 dB away, so a quarter is two halvings: -6 dB.

title: Ohm's law triangle
summary: One rule links voltage (E), current (I) and resistance (R). Know any two and you can find the third.
hook: E on top, I and R below. Cover the one you want: side by side means multiply, one over the other means divide.

title: Power formula: P = I x E
summary: Power is current times voltage. Multiply to get watts, divide watts by volts to get amperes.
hook: Watts are volts times amps: 12 x 2.5 = 30. Going back: 120 / 12 = 10 amperes.

title: Series versus parallel
summary: In series one current flows through everything; in parallel everything shares one voltage. Meters follow the same rule.

points.label: Series circuit
points.value: Current is the same through all components

points.label: Parallel circuit
points.value: Voltage is the same across all components

hook: Voltage is measured across a part (parallel); current is measured through it (series).

title: Powering a radio from DC
summary: Mobile radios run near 12 volts and draw real current, so wiring and battery math matter.

points.label: Battery run time
points.value: Ampere-hour rating divided by average current

title: Radio to computer for digital modes
summary: Digital modes need three signals between radio and computer, with the audio lines crossed over.

points.label: Signals needed
points.value: Receive audio, transmit audio, transmit keying

points.label: Radio audio in and out
points.value: To the computer's audio out and in

hook: Cross them over: radio out goes to computer in, computer out goes to radio in.

title: Receiver controls and what they fix
summary: Each front panel control solves one listening problem.

points.label: Scanning
points.value: Tunes through frequencies to check for activity

points.label: Squelch
points.value: Mutes audio when no signal is present

points.label: Squelch for a weak FM signal
points.value: Set so receiver audio is on all the time

points.label: Filter bandwidth choice
points.value: Match the mode to cut noise and interference

title: Causes of bad audio
summary: Too much audio going in, or tuning slightly off, ruins the sound.

points.label: Too much mic gain on SSB
Talking too loudly on FM
points.value: Audio drops out on voice peaks

title: Resistor, capacitor, inductor
summary: Three basic parts, three jobs: oppose current, store energy in an electric field, store it in a magnetic field.

points.label: Resistor
points.value: Opposes the flow of current in a DC circuit

points.label: Potentiometer
points.value: Adjustable resistance, like a volume control

points.label: Capacitor
points.value: Stores energy in an electric field

points.label: Capacitor build
points.value: Conductive surfaces separated by an insulator

points.label: Inductor
points.value: Stores energy in a magnetic field

points.label: Inductor plus capacitor
points.value: Resonant (tuned) circuit, in series or parallel

hook: Coil means inductor means magnetic field. Plates with an insulator mean capacitor means electric field.

title: Diodes and transistors
summary: A diode is a one-way valve with two leads. A transistor has three and can switch or amplify.

points.label: Diode
points.value: Lets current flow in only one direction

points.label: Diode electrodes
points.value: Anode and cathode; cathode marked with a stripe

points.label: Forward voltage drop
points.value: Lower in some diode types than in others

points.label: LED
points.value: Lights from forward current; visual indicator

points.label: Transistor
points.value: Electronic switch, power gain, three regions

points.label: FET
points.value: Field Effect Transistor: gate, drain, source

hook: Two names for a diode (anode, cathode), three for a transistor: BJT is emitter, base, collector; FET is gate, drain, source.

title: Schematics and figure T-1
summary: A schematic shows how parts connect using standard symbols. Figure T-1 numbers four of them.

points.label: T-1, component 2
points.value: Transistor: controls the flow of current

hook: Read figure T-1 in number order: resistor, transistor, lamp, battery.

title: Figures T-2 and T-3 by number
summary: Learn the numbered parts of figures T-2 and T-3 as a short list, figure by figure.

title: Circuit building blocks
summary: Each block has one job. Name the job and you have the block.

points.label: Transformer (120 V AC)
points.value: Changes it to a lower AC voltage

points.label: Regulator
points.value: Controls the voltage from a power supply

points.label: SPDT switch
points.value: Switches one circuit between two others

points.label: Meter
points.value: Displays a quantity as a numeric value

points.label: Integrated circuit
points.value: Many semiconductors and parts in one package

points.label: Shielded wire
points.value: Stops unwanted signals coupling to or from it

hook: Three power jobs: transformer changes the AC voltage, rectifier turns AC into DC, regulator controls the voltage.

title: Inside a transceiver
summary: A transceiver is a receiver plus a transmitter. A few circuits set, change and carry the frequency.

points.label: Transceiver
points.value: Receiver and transmitter in one device

points.label: Sensitivity
points.value: Ability to detect that a signal is there

points.label: Selectivity
points.value: Ability to pick between multiple signals

points.label: Oscillator
points.value: Generates a signal at a specific frequency

points.label: VFO
points.value: Sets the receive and transmit frequency

points.label: Mixer
points.value: Converts a signal from one frequency to another

points.label: Transverter
points.value: Converts transceiver RF to another band

points.label: Modulation
points.value: Combining speech with an RF carrier

hook: Sensitivity senses (is a signal there?); selectivity selects (which signal?).

title: Test equipment: what each measures
summary: Match each instrument to the one thing it tells you.

points.label: Antenna analyzer
points.value: Is the antenna resonant on your frequency

points.label: Dummy load: purpose
points.value: Test without transmitting over the air

points.label: Dummy load: build
points.value: 50-ohm non-inductive resistor on a heat sink

title: Using an ohmmeter safely
summary: An ohmmeter supplies its own small current, so measure only with the circuit unpowered.

points.label: How it works
points.value: Applies a small current, measures the voltage

points.label: In-circuit resistance
points.value: Make sure the circuit is not powered

points.label: Damages the meter
points.value: Measuring voltage on the resistance setting

title: SWR: how well things match
summary: SWR measures how well a load is matched to its feed line. 1:1 is perfect; higher readings mean mismatch.

points.label: What SWR measures
points.value: How well a load is matched to a feed line

points.label: High SWR
points.value: Low RF output from a solid-state transceiver

points.label: Why power drops
points.value: To protect the RF output amplifier transistors

points.label: Erratic SWR
points.value: Loose connection in antenna or feed line

points.label: Antenna tuner
points.value: Matches antenna system to transceiver impedance

title: Interference: problem and fix
summary: Each interference problem has a matching first fix. Learn them as pairs.

points.label: FM over-deviating
points.value: Talk farther away from the microphone

points.label: Distorted voice
points.value: Clip-on ferrite choke on the microphone cable

points.label: Neighbor complains
points.value: Check your rig and your own TV for interference

points.label: Broadcast radio hears you
points.value: It can't reject strong signals outside its band

points.label: Neighbor's receiver
points.value: Filter at the affected receiver's antenna input

points.label: Cable TV, first step
points.value: Check TV coax connectors are installed properly

hook: Fix your own audio first, then block the signal where it gets in: filters at receiver inputs, good coax connectors.

title: Signal bandwidth, narrow to wide
summary: Modes line up from narrowest to widest: CW, SSB, FM, then TV.
hook: 150 Hz, 3 kHz, 10 to 15 kHz, 6 MHz: each step up is at least three times wider than the one before.

title: FM versus SSB: where each is used
summary: FM (or PM) is the repeater and packet mode. SSB, a form of AM, is the VHF and UHF weak signal voice mode.

points.label: FM drawback
points.value: Only one signal can be received at a time

title: Mode and network names decoded
summary: Many mode questions just ask what a name or abbreviation means. Learn each one as a pair.

points.label: FT8
points.value: Digital mode for low signal-to-noise operation

points.label: DMR
points.value: Two digital voices on one 12.5 kHz channel

points.label: APRS
points.value: Real-time tactical data with a station map

points.label: ARQ
points.value: Receiver detects errors, asks for a resend

points.label: Mesh network
points.value: Commercial Wi-Fi gear with modified firmware

title: Satellite basics
summary: Satellite questions cover the beacon, the uplink and downlink bands, and why the signal shifts and fades.

points.label: Beacon
points.value: Health and status telemetry; anyone may receive

points.label: Right uplink power
points.value: Downlink about the same as the beacon

points.label: LEO
points.value: Low Earth Orbit, period around 100 minutes

points.label: Spin fading
points.value: Rotation of the satellite and its antennas

hook: Use the beacon as your yardstick: match its downlink strength and you are neither too low nor too high.

title: Internet linking: IRLP, EchoLink
summary: Several systems carry ham voice over the internet. Know how each is reached.

points.label: VoIP
points.value: Voice over the internet using digital techniques

points.label: IRLP
points.value: Connects repeaters and systems via internet

points.label: EchoLink
points.value: Use a repeater without a radio

points.label: Before using EchoLink
points.value: Register call sign, provide proof of license

points.label: Gateway
points.value: Station connecting others to the internet

title: Operating activities
summary: Hunting signals and contesting, plus the grid locator, a short code for where a station is.

points.label: Contesting
points.value: Contact as many stations as possible in a period

points.label: Contest good practice
points.value: Send only the minimum ID and exchange

points.label: Grid locator
points.value: Letter-number code for a geographic location

title: Antenna length and frequency
summary: Antenna length sets its frequency. Shorter means higher, and inductors make it act longer.

points.label: Loading
points.value: Inserting inductors to lengthen it electrically

points.label: Short flexible handheld whip
points.value: Low efficiency next to a full quarter-wave

points.label: 5/8-wave versus 1/4-wave
points.value: The longer whip has more gain

title: Antenna direction and gain
summary: Gain means more signal in one direction than a reference antenna. Polarization is the electric field's orientation.

points.label: Antenna gain
points.value: More signal one way, compared to a reference

title: Feed line loss ranking
summary: Coax is the everyday feed line. Loss climbs with frequency and drops with better cable.

points.label: Why coax is most common
points.value: Easy to use, few special installation needs

points.label: Foam versus solid dielectric
points.value: Foam has less loss per foot

points.label: RG-213 versus RG-58
points.value: RG-213 has less loss at a given frequency

title: Coax connectors and water
summary: Pick the connector for the frequency, then keep water out: it is coax's main enemy.

points.label: Outdoors: PL259, BNC, Type N
points.value: Tape all of them for weather protection

points.label: UV resistant jacket
points.value: UV damage lets water into the cable

title: Shock, fire and stored energy
summary: Fuses guard the hot wire, and batteries and capacitors hold energy that can hurt you.

points.label: Fuse purpose
points.value: Removes power in case of an overload

points.label: Where a fuse goes
points.value: In series with the hot conductor only

points.label: 5 A fuse swapped for 20 A
points.value: Excessive current could cause a fire

points.label: Measuring high voltage
points.value: Meter and leads rated for that voltage

hook: Black is hot, and the fuse goes on the hot wire. Never fit a bigger fuse than the circuit was built for.

title: Grounding and lightning protection
summary: Good grounds are short, direct, free of sharp bends, and all bonded together.

points.label: External ground rods
points.value: Bond together with heavy wire or strap

points.label: Tower ground
points.value: Separate eight-foot rod per leg, all bonded

points.label: Lightning arrester
points.value: Grounded panel near where feed lines enter

title: Tower and antenna safety
summary: Power lines are the main danger when putting up antennas, and nobody climbs alone.

points.label: Overhead wires
points.value: Look for them and stay clear

points.label: Distance from power lines
points.value: If it falls, stays 10 feet from the wires

points.label: Crank-up tower
points.value: Climb only retracted or with safety locks

hook: Power lines first: stay clear, allow 10 feet even if it falls, skip utility poles.

title: RF exposure basics
summary: Radio waves are non-ionizing, but the body absorbs them, and the licensee keeps exposure within limits.

points.label: Unlike radioactivity
points.value: Not enough energy to damage DNA

points.label: Why limits vary
points.value: Body absorbs more at some frequencies

title: Duty cycle and exposure
summary: Duty cycle is how much of the time you transmit. Less transmit time means less average exposure.

points.label: Duty cycle
points.value: Percentage of time the transmitter transmits

hook: Halve the time on the air (100 to 50 percent) and the allowed power density doubles.
